items.title: Doc Cheatham interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, New York City, New York, July 28, 1995
items.q: And every big band I played from Chick Webb, Sam Wooding, everybody, lead.

ctx.x: That’s a good point. Well I think that might have been the case with your friend in California where after you hear young students for so long, your ears get desensitized to, like playing in tune.

Yes. Absolutely. I realized that right quick and I gave up. Oh boy. I’m going out playing with different groups and things like that, sitting in. As far as being a trumpet player, I was always playing as a lead trumpet player. I wasn’t a soloist in big bands, I was a lead player. And every big band I played from Chick Webb, Sam Wooding, everybody, lead. Because no one wanted to play lead. The trumpet players didn’t want to play lead when I first came around. They didn’t want to lead, even from the Preservation…

items.title: 54270_Doc Cheatham oral history interview
items.q: I joined Chick Webb's band, I went there that night... and the book, so naturally I went and sat, and played the lead.

ctx.x: But when did you first become aware of the fact that there were writers writing about jazz, books out on the subject and so forth? You must've become aware of that in the '30's, didn't you?

I did because that -- was one book I have, I think I have the book where there was -- an Esquire jazz book I think in the '30's, where they said Doc Cheatham the greatest first trumpet player in the world, and I didn't like that. Cause I didn't want to be called a first trumpet player. Benny Carter had a write-up somewhere, recently, a few years ago, that he said Doc Cheatham's the greatest first trumpet -- was, at that time, greatest trumpet player in the world. And I didn't like that I didn't want to be branded…

I joined Chick Webb's band, I went there that night, there was Freddie Jenkins, I don't know what other trumpet player but they all sat down and left the first trumpet chair open and nobody seated there. And the book, so naturally I went and sat, and played the lead.
